label: The CP System
note: Proposed text was 'The CP System, later called CPS-1'; the link wraps only the name, 'The CP System', so that the surrounding words stay plain.
before: The CP System, later called CPS-1, ran a 68000 at 10 MHz for the game and a Z80 at 3.58 MHz for sound, with two custom graphics chips, CPS-A and CPS-B. Its picture was 384 × 224 pixels, wider than the 320 of the Mega Drive and the Neo Geo or the 256 of the Super NES. *Forgotten Worlds* and *[Strider](/vault/games/strider)* came first, in 1988 and 1989, then *[Final Fight](/vault/games/final-fight)*, and in 1991 *[Street Fighter II](/vault/games/street-fighter-ii)*. By Sanglard's count Capcom released more than thirty games on the board between 1988 and 1995.

label: the CP System
note: Proposed text was 'the CP System, a standard board'; the link wraps only the name, 'the CP System', so that the surrounding words stay plain.
before: In 1988, as *3DO Magazine* later put it, Capcom's research division "revolutionised the arcades". *The Games Machine* reported in June 1989 that it had spent two and a half years and £5.5 million developing a "super chip" that compressed "the power of ten normal arcade circuit boards into two microchips", so that operators could change games in a cabinet more easily. The result was the CP System, a standard board on which each new game ran. *Forgotten Worlds* was the first. *Strider*, *Ghouls 'n Ghosts*, *UN Squadron* and *Final Fight* followed, and so did *Street Fighter II*. In 1993 a second board, CPS II, made its debut with *Super Street Fighter II*.

label: CP System board
before: Most heroes in 1989's arcades ran and jumped. Strider Hiryu cartwheeled, slid along the floor under bullets, raced down slopes, and clamped himself to walls and ceilings to fight upside down. *CRASH*'s arcade reviewer watched him "do a triple backflip while slicing a robot in half with his laser sword" and decided it was "some of the most demanding gameplay ever invented – it's exhausting just to watch!" The game was among the first to run on Capcom's new CP System board, and its creator, Kouichi Yotsui, took its name from Tolkien's *The Lord of the Rings*.

label: CP System arcade board

label: CP System hardware
before: Arcade hardware drew the scenery in layers as well as the sprites, which gave designers a second tool. In Capcom's *[Final Fight](/vault/games/final-fight)* (1989), as Fabien Sanglard's study of the CP System hardware shows, the characters, tyres and barrels all share one sprite layer, so which of them hides which is a matter of sprite order. To let the fighters pass behind part of the scenery, as they do on the stairs near the end of the first round, the hardware let individual background tiles mark some of their colours as drawn in front of the sprites.

label: Odyssey
note: Proposed text was 'the Odyssey, the first video game console for the home'; the link wraps only the name, 'Odyssey', so that the surrounding words stay plain.
before: In 1966 some forty million American homes had a television set, and every one of them could only show what the broadcasters sent. Ralph Baer, chief engineer for equipment design at a defence contractor in New Hampshire, wanted to plug something into them that people could play. Six years later Magnavox sold his idea as the Odyssey, the first video game console for the home. Along the way, the patents that came out of his lab made [Atari](/vault/companies/atari) and many others pay for the right to put a bouncing ball on a screen.

label: Odyssey
note: Proposed text was 'the Odyssey in 1972'; the link wraps only the name, 'Odyssey', so that the surrounding words stay plain.
before: Bushnell had not invented video table tennis. At Sanders Associates in New Hampshire, [Ralph Baer](/vault/people/ralph-baer) and his colleagues William Rusch and William Harrison had worked out TV games in the 1960s and patented them, and Magnavox began making their design as the Odyssey in 1972. Its games, in Baer's words, were "a line down the middle to indicate the net, and paddles and balls". In May 1972 Magnavox took the Odyssey on a tour of dealers, and on 24 May, at Burlingame, California, Bushnell played its ping-pong and handball games for about half an hour. In court he later recalled telling Nutting that it was "a home unit, not very interesting to play, no competition".

before: Guns that fired light at targets came first. The arcade maker Seeburg sold a shooting game called the Ray-O-Lite in 1936. The first video light gun came out of Ralph Baer's work at Sanders Associates in the 1960s. His team built a "light pen" for quiz games, then turned it into a gun, and by June 1967 their TV Game Unit 2 had a target-shooting game played with two of them. When Baer's design became the Magnavox Odyssey in 1972, the gun was the only accessory ever made for its expansion port. In the Odyssey's Shooting Gallery, the player fired at a square of light bouncing across an overlay on the television screen.

before: The first analogue controls in the home were knobs. *Edge*'s 1996 history of controllers noted that the first home systems "were dedicated ping pong machines controlled with twisting knobs", and the [paddle controller](/vault/hardware/paddle-controller) entry follows that line from the Magnavox Odyssey and *[Pong](/vault/games/pong)* to the Atari VCS and the home computers. A paddle tells the program where the player wants the bat to be, not which way it is moving. A joystick built the same way does that in two directions at once: a potentiometer on each axis, which, in *Edge*'s words, "changes the amount of current running from the stick to the computer, enabling the computer to know exactly how far and in what direction the joystick has been moved." PC [flight sticks](/vault/hardware/flight-stick) worked like this from the 1980s onwards.
